---
title: "Choosing a sampling method"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# here() would stop at analysis/, which has its own _quarto.yml. Declaring
# this file's place in the repo fixes the root at the repository itself.
here::i_am("analysis/sampling-design.qmd")
source(here::here("scripts", "00_setup.R"))
source(here::here("analysis", "_common.R"))   # data, provisional choices, Draft B
library(BalancedSampling)   # local pivotal method; install + renv::snapshot()

# ---- choices this chapter makes, all provisional ----------------------------
N_CHASED <- 1000      # chased (Lucky Dip) sample size
N_REPS   <- 500       # simulated draws per design
MIN_PER_CELL <- 2     # stratified design: fewest towers per cell
FRAME_RING_LABELS <- c("4-5", "6-7", "8-9", "10+")   # the frame starts at 4 bells
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate
#| include: false
# ---- synthetic population built from 1988's published rates ----------------
# 1988 Tables 9.2 and 9.3: share of towers with a band, and ringers per bell
# where there is a band, by settlement type. Table 9.2 also by ring size.
rates_1988 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~type_1988,   ~band_pct, ~ringers_per_bell,
  "Inner City",  63,        1.22,
  "Suburban",    92,        1.45,
  "Large City",  92,        1.70,
  "Town",        92,        1.42,
  "Village",     70,        1.24
)
band_by_bells_1988 <- c(`3` = 55, `4-5` = 55, `6-7` = 86, `8-9` = 92, `10+` = 95)
BAND_ALL_1988 <- 78   # "there was a band at 78 per cent of the surveyed towers"

villages <- c("Village", "Small village or hamlet")

pop <- frame_towers |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ring_class = droplevels(.data$ring_class)
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(rates_1988, by = "type_1988") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Combine the settlement-type and ring-size rates on the log-odds scale,
    # centred on the 1988 overall rate.
    p_step = stats::plogis(stats::qlogis(.data$band_pct / 100) +
                           stats::qlogis(band_by_bells_1988[as.character(.data$ring_class)] / 100) -
                           stats::qlogis(BAND_ALL_1988 / 100)),
    rpb_step = .data$ringers_per_bell
  )

# Second stand-in: the same 1988 pattern, but expressed smoothly in the
# continuous measures instead of in steps at the type boundaries. Fitted by
# regressing the step rates on the measures.
smooth_terms <- ~ ld + u + isolation + log(bells)
p_fit   <- stats::glm(stats::update(smooth_terms, p_step ~ .), data = pop,
                      family = stats::quasibinomial())
rpb_fit <- stats::lm(stats::update(smooth_terms, rpb_step ~ .), data = pop)
pop$p_smooth   <- stats::fitted(p_fit)
pop$rpb_smooth <- pmax(0.5, stats::fitted(rpb_fit))

make_outcome <- function(p, rpb) {
  has_band <- stats::rbinom(length(p), 1, p)
  ringers  <- has_band * stats::rpois(length(p), pop$bells * rpb *
                                        stats::rgamma(length(p), shape = 4, rate = 4))
  list(has_band = has_band, ringers = ringers)
}
outcomes <- list(
  "Steps at type boundaries"   = make_outcome(pop$p_step,   pop$rpb_step),
  "Smooth in the measures"     = make_outcome(pop$p_smooth, pop$rpb_smooth)
)

xy <- sf::sf_project("OGC:CRS84", "ESRI:54009", cbind(pop$lon, pop$lat))
pop$east <- xy[, 1]; pop$north <- xy[, 2]

N <- nrow(pop); n <- N_CHASED
in_village <- pop$type %in% villages

truth_of <- function(o) c(
  total_ringers    = sum(o$ringers),
  share_with_band  = mean(o$has_band),
  ringers_per_bell = sum(o$ringers) / sum(pop$bells),
  village_ringers  = sum(o$ringers[in_village])
)

estimate <- function(o, s, pi) {
  w <- 1 / pi[s]
  c(total_ringers    = sum(w * o$ringers[s]),
    share_with_band  = sum(w * o$has_band[s]) / sum(w),
    ringers_per_bell = sum(w * o$ringers[s]) / sum(w * pop$bells[s]),
    village_ringers  = sum(w * o$ringers[s] * in_village[s]))
}

# Tower clusters are one stratum whatever their type and ring size: shared
# bands make ring size a poor guide there (D-036).
pop$stratum_type <- ifelse(pop$tower_cluster, "Tower cluster", as.character(pop$type))
pop$ring_stratum <- ifelse(pop$tower_cluster, "all", as.character(pop$ring_class))
strata <- interaction(pop$stratum_type, pop$ring_stratum, drop = TRUE)
Nh <- table(strata)
nh <- pmin(Nh, pmax(MIN_PER_CELL, round(n * Nh / N)))
pi_strat <- as.numeric((nh / Nh)[as.character(strata)])

# Sort order for the systematic design: type, then ring class, then density,
# reversing direction in alternate groups ("serpentine") so neighbours in the
# list stay similar across group boundaries.
grp <- as.integer(interaction(pop$stratum_type, pop$ring_stratum, lex.order = TRUE, drop = TRUE))
sys_order <- order(grp, ifelse(grp %% 2 == 0, -1, 1) * log10(pop[[LOCAL_VAR]] + 1))

# Place measures plus ring size. "Growth since the bells" is left out: it is
# computed from ring size, so it would carry ring size in twice.
spread_cov <- scale(cbind(log10(pop[[LOCAL_VAR]] + 1), log10(pop[[REGION_VAR]] + 1),
                          pop$isolation, pop$coast, log(pop$bells)))
spread_geo <- cbind(spread_cov, scale(cbind(pop$east, pop$north)))
stopifnot("spread measures must be complete" = all(is.finite(spread_geo)))

designs <- list(
  "Simple random"                = \() list(s = sample.int(N, n), pi = rep(n / N, N)),
  "Stratified: type x ring size" = \() {
    s <- unlist(lapply(names(Nh), \(h) {
      idx <- which(strata == h); idx[sample.int(length(idx), nh[[h]])] }))
    list(s = s, pi = pi_strat)
  },
  "Sorted systematic"            = \() {
    k <- N / n; start <- stats::runif(1, 0, k)
    pos <- floor(start + k * (0:(n - 1))) + 1
    list(s = sys_order[pos], pi = rep(n / N, N))
  },
  "Spread: measures only"        = \() list(s = lpm2(rep(n / N, N), spread_cov), pi = rep(n / N, N)),
  "Spread: measures + map"       = \() list(s = lpm2(rep(n / N, N), spread_geo), pi = rep(n / N, N))
)

# Each design is drawn N_REPS times; every draw is scored against both
# stand-in populations.
sims <- purrr::imap(designs, \(draw, name) {
  purrr::map(seq_len(N_REPS), \(r) {
    d <- draw()
    purrr::imap(outcomes, \(o, pop_name) tibble::tibble(
      design = name, population = pop_name, rep = r,
      measure = names(truth_of(o)), estimate = estimate(o, d$s, d$pi),
      truth = truth_of(o),
      n_drawn = length(d$s),
      small_drawn = sum(pop$type[d$s] == "Small village or hamlet"))) |>
      purrr::list_rbind()
  }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()

perf <- sims |>
  dplyr::summarise(rmse = sqrt(mean((.data$estimate - .data$truth)^2)),
                   bias = mean(.data$estimate - .data$truth),
                   .by = c("population", "design", "measure")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_rmse = .data$rmse / .data$rmse[.data$design == "Simple random"],
                .by = c("population", "measure"))

# The design with the lowest average relative error across both populations
# and all four measures.
design_rank <- perf |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$design != "Simple random") |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_rel = mean(.data$rel_rmse), worst_rel = max(.data$rel_rmse),
                   .by = "design") |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$mean_rel)
robust_design <- design_rank$design[[1]]

# Stratum cells: type x ring size (tower clusters as one stratum).
cells <- pop |>
  dplyr::count(type = factor(.data$stratum_type, levels = c(TYPE_LEVELS, "Tower cluster")), ring_class = factor(.data$ring_stratum,
                                               levels = c(levels(pop$ring_class), "all"))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(expected = .data$n / N * N_CHASED)
n_cells_small <- sum(cells$expected < 10)
```

*Prepared by Mark Ainsworth with Claude (Anthropic). Mark set the questions
and made the decisions; Claude drafted the code and text, which Mark
reviewed.*

## Where this stands

*Mark's take, drafted by Claude from Mark's decisions. Tentative: to be
tested with the other analysis volunteers.*

**Current recommendation.** Draw the chased sample stratified by place type
and ring size, with proportional allocation:

- Strata are the seven place types from *Choosing a classification*,
  crossed with ring size (4–5, 6–7, 8–9, 10+).
- Cells expecting fewer than about 10 chased towers are merged with a
  neighbour of the same ring size (a centre with its suburb, for example).
- Towers in tower clusters form one stratum, whatever their type and ring
  size, because their shared bands make ring size a poor guide there.
- Results are reported by place type crossed with ring size, which maps onto
  1988's tables.

**Why stratified, when the designs are close.** In the simulation it had the
lowest average error, and the designs that use the types are within noise of
each other. It is the easiest to explain to delegates ("we drew X villages
with six bells"), it matches the implementation design's "stratified by
bells x rurality", and its variance estimation is standard.

**Still open.**

1. *Re-run this simulation on the full context data* (script 08 as run on
   Mark's machine), with the settled lines.
2. *The exact merging of small cells*, to fix before the draw.
3. *Whether to over-sample the small villages and hamlets.* If they hold
   most of the towers without a band, more of them would sharpen that
   estimate, at the cost of unequal weights. The current plan says no.

## Background and brief

**Where this fits.** The census will chase about `r fmt(N_CHASED)` randomly
drawn towers until each replies. Comparing them with towers that reply
unprompted shows who does not respond, and lets the estimates correct for
it. The chapter *Choosing a classification* gives each tower a place type,
built from place measures only. This chapter asks how to use the types,
the measures and ring size when drawing the chased sample.

**What Mark asked for.**

- *Stratify by number of bells and by type of place*, or by something that
  achieves the same.
- *Align with good, defensible practice*, and explain it to delegates.
- *Pay heed to 1988*, which drew a simple random sample of 500 towers.

**What this chapter uses.** The working classification (Draft B), and the
1988 survey's published rates to build stand-in populations. Both are
provisional, so the comparison between designs matters more than any single
number.

**What it does not decide.** The design itself, which is open question Q-023.

## Headline findings

- **The best design was `r robust_design`.** Over `r N_REPS` simulated
  draws of `r fmt(N_CHASED)` towers, scored against two stand-in
  populations, it had `r pct(abs(1 - design_rank$mean_rel[[1]]))`
  `r if (design_rank$mean_rel[[1]] < 1) "less" else "more"` error than
  simple random sampling, on average across four estimates.
- **The gains are modest, and the designs are close.** Average error,
  relative to simple random sampling, runs from
  `r round(min(design_rank$mean_rel), 2)` to
  `r round(max(design_rank$mean_rel), 2)`. Practical differences
  (explanation, variance estimation, cell sizes) should weigh as much as the
  error figures.
- **Stratifying by type and ring size makes small cells.** Of
  `r nrow(cells)` cells, `r n_cells_small` expect fewer than 10 chased towers
  under proportional allocation, and would need merging for stable
  estimates.

## Which sampling design? A simulation

**The question.** For the chased sample of `r fmt(N_CHASED)` towers, which
way of drawing gives the most accurate estimates? Five designs are compared:

| Design | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Simple random | Every set of towers equally likely. The baseline, and what 1988 did |
| Stratified: type x ring size | Fixed numbers from each combination of place type and ring-size class, in proportion to its size, at least `r MIN_PER_CELL` each |
| Sorted systematic | List the towers by type, ring size and density, then take every k-th from a random start |
| Spread: measures only | Local pivotal method:^[Grafström, Lundström & Schelin (2012).] towers similar in density, isolation, coast and ring size compete, so the sample spreads evenly across those measures |
| Spread: measures + map | The same, with map position added, so the sample also spreads across the country |

All five give every tower the same chance of selection, apart from the small
departures that the stratified design's minimum per cell creates.

**The test population.** The true number of ringers at each tower is
unknown until the census, so a stand-in is built from 1988's published
rates. Each tower gets a band with a probability set by its 1988 settlement
type and ring size (1988 Table 9.2), and a band size set by its ring size and
1988's ringers per bell for its type (Table 9.3), plus random variation. The
place types are mapped to 1988's five as in *Choosing a classification*. This
is not a forecast. Its only job is to have the right *kind* of structure, so
the designs can be compared fairly.

Two versions are used, because the answer depends on the shape of the truth:

- **Steps at type boundaries:** rates change only between types and
  ring-size classes, exactly as 1988's tables are laid out. This favours
  designs that use the types.
- **Smooth in the measures:** the same overall pattern, but varying
  smoothly with density, growth since the bells, isolation and ring size.
  This favours designs that spread across the measures.

A design that does well under both is the safe choice.

```{r}
#| label: fig-designs
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Error of each design relative to a simple random sample (1 = same error; lower is better), over repeated simulated draws. Rows: the two stand-in populations."
labels <- c(total_ringers = "Total ringers", share_with_band = "Share of towers with a band",
            ringers_per_bell = "Ringers per bell", village_ringers = "Ringers in villages and hamlets")
perf |>
  dplyr::mutate(measure = factor(labels[.data$measure], levels = labels),
                design = factor(.data$design, levels = names(designs))) |>
  ggplot(aes(rel_rmse, design)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL_CAT[1], size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(population ~ measure, labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 16)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0)) +
  labs(x = "Error relative to simple random sampling (root mean square)", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-designs
perf |>
  dplyr::mutate(measure = labels[.data$measure], rel_rmse = round(.data$rel_rmse, 2)) |>
  dplyr::select("population", "design", "measure", "rel_rmse") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "measure", values_from = "rel_rmse") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Relative error by design (simple random = 1)")

design_rank |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c("mean_rel", "worst_rel"), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  dplyr::rename(`average relative error` = "mean_rel", `worst relative error` = "worst_rel") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Designs ranked by average relative error across both populations and all four estimates")
```

**Fair shares.** A worry about any design without fixed quotas is that a
type could end up under-represented by chance. The table shows how many
small villages and hamlets each design draws:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-small-counts
sims |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$measure == "total_ringers",
                .data$population == names(outcomes)[1]) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `drawn: average` = round(mean(.data$small_drawn)),
    `drawn: range in 95% of draws` = paste(
      round(stats::quantile(.data$small_drawn, 0.025)), "to",
      round(stats::quantile(.data$small_drawn, 0.975))),
    .by = "design"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Small villages and hamlets in each draw of ", fmt(N_CHASED),
                                " (fair share: ", round(N_CHASED * type_share[["Small village or hamlet"]]), ")"))
```

**Why the gains are modest.** The stand-ins inherit 1988's rates, and those
barely differ outside the villages: towns, suburbs and large cities all had
a band at 92% of towers. A design can only gain from differences that
exist. If the census finds bigger contrasts, for example between small
villages and larger ones, the gains from using the types will be bigger.

**How precise the comparison is.** Each relative error comes from
`r N_REPS` simulated draws, so it is uncertain by about
±`r round(2 / sqrt(N_REPS), 2)` (95%). Designs closer than that cannot be
told apart, and their order in the ranking may change from run to run.

**The strongest case against trusting these numbers.** Both stand-in
populations were built from the same types and measures the designs use.
That flatters every design that uses them. Real gains will be smaller, and
will depend on how strongly real band size and response follow these
measures. What should hold is the comparison between designs, which is why
two differently shaped populations are used.

## Stratum cells

If the draw is stratified by type and ring size, each cell needs enough
chased towers for a stable estimate: about 10 is a common rule of thumb, and
at least 2 are needed to estimate variance at all. The table shows the frame
count in each cell, and in brackets the chased towers expected under
proportional allocation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cells
cells |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(.data$n, " (", round(.data$expected), ")")) |>
  dplyr::select("type", "ring_class", "cell") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = "ring_class", values_from = "cell", values_fill = "",
                     names_sort = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$type) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste0("Frame towers by type and ring size (expected chased towers at n = ", fmt(N_CHASED), ")"))
```

The small cells are mostly the urban types with small rings. They can be
merged with their neighbours (a centre with its suburb, for example), or
drawn as one stratum regardless of ring size, as the tower clusters are.

## Practical differences the simulation does not show

| Design | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stratified | Easiest to explain: "we drew X villages" | Many small cells once crossed with ring size; cells need at least 2 for variance estimation, so some must be merged |
| Sorted systematic | Near-exact fair shares with no cells; close in spirit to 1988's alphabetical list | Variance estimation needs an approximation, usually pairing neighbouring draws |
| Spread (local pivotal) | Uses the continuous measures directly; can spread across the map too | Least familiar to delegates; needs the `BalancedSampling` package and its variance estimator |

1988's own sampling bears on this. It drew "500, picked at random from all
of the towers listed in an updated computer version of Dove's guide,
arranged alphabetically", and checked afterwards that ring sizes and regions
were fairly represented. The settlement types were used for analysis, not
for drawing the sample.

## Methods and sources

**Spread and balanced sampling.** Grafström, A., Lundström, N. L. P. &
Schelin, L. (2012), "Spatially balanced sampling through the pivotal
method", *Biometrics* 68(2), 514–520. Deville, J.-C. & Tillé, Y. (2004),
"Efficient balanced sampling: the cube method", *Biometrika* 91(4),
893–912. Grafström, A. & Schelin, L. (2014), "How to select representative
samples", *Scandinavian Journal of Statistics* 41(2), 277–290, gives the
variance estimator for spread samples. All three are implemented in the R
package `BalancedSampling`.

**1988.** *The Central Council Survey of Ringing* (1988 survey, published in
*The Ringing World* 1989 and collected as a book). Chapter 2 (sampling),
Chapter 4 (bands) and Chapter 9 (geography, Tables 9.1–9.3).
